name: Sodium chloride (table salt)

bonding.summary: A cubic lattice of Na+ and Cl− ions, each surrounded by six of the other.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives its single outer electron to chlorine (Δχ 2.23). Na+ now has neon's electron arrangement and Cl− has argon's. The ions share nothing; they simply attract.

facts: Salt crystals are cubes because the ions stack in a cubic pattern.
A violent reaction between a soft metal and a poisonous gas gives harmless table salt.
summary: Table salt is the classic ionic compound: sodium hands an electron to chlorine and the ions lock into a cube.

name: Potassium chloride

bonding.summary: K+ and Cl− ions in the rock-salt arrangement.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium gives its 4s electron to chlorine; both ions end up with argon's electron arrangement.

occurrence: Mined from sylvite and potash deposits.
facts: About 95% of potash is used as fertilizer.
hazards: Safe in food amounts; dangerous if injected.
summary: KCl is the main potassium fertilizer and a low-sodium salt substitute.

name: Lithium fluoride

bonding.summary: Small Li+ and F− ions packed tightly in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Lithium gives its 2s electron to fluorine (Δχ 3.0), one of the most ionic bonds possible.

facts: LiF transmits ultraviolet light down to about 105 nm, further than any other common crystal.
summary: LiF is one of the most ionic compounds, valued for UV optics and radiation detectors.

name: Potassium bromide

bonding.summary: K+ and Br− ions in the rock-salt arrangement.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium transfers one electron to bromine.

uses: Pellets and windows for infrared spectroscopy
facts: In the 1800s KBr was a common sedative, the origin of the phrase 'take a bromide'.
summary: KBr is transparent to infrared light, so chemists press it into pellets to analyze samples.

name: Rubidium chloride

bonding.summary: Rb+ and Cl− ions in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Rubidium gives up its single 5s electron to chlorine.

uses: Rubidium-82 chloride for heart PET scans
Making competent bacteria in molecular biology
facts: Under pressure RbCl switches to the cesium chloride structure.
summary: RbCl is a simple salt; its radioactive form Rb-82 chloride images blood flow in the heart.

name: Silver chloride

bonding.summary: Rock-salt lattice with partly covalent bonds, which makes it insoluble in water.
bonding.electronSharing: Silver gives one electron to chlorine, but Ag+ distorts the chloride's electron cloud, so some sharing remains.

occurrence: The mineral chlorargyrite; formed in tests for chloride.
facts: Photochromic lenses darken in sunlight because AgCl crystals release silver atoms.
summary: AgCl darkens in light, the property behind early photography and self-tinting glasses.

name: Silver bromide

bonding.summary: Rock-salt lattice with partial covalent character.
bonding.electronSharing: Silver gives one electron to bromine. Light can push an electron back from Br− to Ag+, forming silver atoms: the basis of photography.

facts: A few silver atoms formed by light make a 'latent image' that developer turns into a visible picture.
summary: AgBr is the light-sensitive heart of photographic film.

name: Magnesium oxide

bonding.summary: Doubly charged Mg2+ and O2− ions in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Magnesium gives two electrons to oxygen. The double charges make the attraction very strong, so MgO melts at 2,852 °C.

formation: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO (the white ash of burning magnesium)
occurrence: The mineral periclase; made from magnesite or seawater.
facts: With doubly charged ions, MgO's lattice energy (about 3,800 kJ/mol) is nearly five times NaCl's.
summary: MgO is a very high-melting ionic solid that lines furnaces.

name: Calcium oxide (quicklime)

bonding.summary: Ca2+ and O2− ions in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons to oxygen.

occurrence: Made in lime kilns from limestone.
facts: Heated quicklime glows brightly: the 'limelight' that lit 19th-century theaters.
hazards: Caustic; reacts with water releasing heat.
summary: Quicklime is made by baking limestone and is the starting point of cement.

name: Lead(II) sulfide (galena)

bonding.summary: Rock-salt structure, but with substantial covalent sharing; it is a semiconductor.
bonding.electronSharing: Lead and sulfur have similar electronegativities (Δχ 0.25), so electrons are shared rather than fully transferred, leaving a small band gap.

formation: Natural mineral; Pb2+ + H2S -> PbS + 2 H+
facts: Galena crystals were the first semiconductor devices, used in crystal radios around 1906.
summary: Galena is the shiny grey cubic ore of lead and an early semiconductor.

name: Cesium chloride

bonding.summary: Each large Cs+ ion sits at the center of a cube of eight Cl− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Cesium gives its 6s electron to chlorine. Because Cs+ is large it can fit eight neighbors instead of six.

facts: The Meselson–Stahl experiment of 1958 used a CsCl gradient to prove how DNA copies itself.
summary: CsCl gives its name to a crystal structure in which each ion has eight neighbors.

name: Calcium fluoride (fluorite)

bonding.summary: Ca2+ ions on a face-centered cubic lattice with F− ions filling all the tetrahedral holes.
bonding.electronSharing: Each calcium gives one electron to each of two fluorines.

occurrence: The mineral fluorite, in many colors.
uses: Lenses for UV, infrared and high-end cameras
facts: The word 'fluorescence' comes from fluorite, which glows under UV light.
summary: Fluorite gives its name to both a crystal structure and to fluorescence.

name: Zinc sulfide (sphalerite)

bonding.summary: Each Zn bonded tetrahedrally to four S, like diamond with two kinds of atoms.
bonding.electronSharing: Zinc and sulfur share electron pairs in four directional bonds, pulled toward sulfur (Δχ 0.93).

formation: Natural mineral; Zn2+ + H2S -> ZnS + 2 H+
facts: Copper-doped ZnS was the classic glow-in-the-dark material; it sublimes near 1,185 °C at normal pressure.
summary: Sphalerite names the zincblende structure used by many semiconductors.

name: Zirconium dioxide (cubic zirconia)

bonding.summary: Zr4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure (cubic form, stabilized by yttrium).
bonding.electronSharing: Zirconium gives four electrons, two to each of two oxygens, with some covalent character.

occurrence: Rare mineral baddeleyite; made from zircon.
facts: Pure ZrO2 is monoclinic; a little yttria locks it into the sparkling cubic form.
summary: Cubic zirconia is a tough, sparkling ceramic used as imitation diamond and in oxygen sensors.

name: Cerium(IV) oxide

bonding.summary: Ce4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Cerium gives four electrons to oxygen. It can easily take one back (Ce3+), releasing oxygen, which makes ceria an oxygen 'sponge'.

occurrence: Made from monazite and bastnäsite ores.
facts: Ceria is the standard powder for polishing optical glass to a flawless finish.
summary: Ceria polishes glass and helps catalytic converters by storing and releasing oxygen.

name: Thorium dioxide

bonding.summary: Th4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Thorium gives four electrons to oxygen.

occurrence: The mineral thorianite; from monazite sand.
facts: ThO2 has the highest melting point of any oxide, 3,350 °C.
summary: Thoria is the highest-melting oxide known and glows brightly in lantern mantles.

name: Uranium dioxide

bonding.summary: U4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Uranium gives four electrons to oxygen, keeping two 5f electrons.

occurrence: The mineral uraninite (pitchblende); made for fuel.
uses: Nuclear fuel pellets in almost all power reactors
facts: A fuel pellet the size of a fingertip releases as much energy as about a tonne of coal.
summary: UO2 ceramic pellets are the fuel of nearly every nuclear power plant.

name: Neptunium dioxide

bonding.summary: Np4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Neptunium gives four electrons to oxygen.

uses: Target for making plutonium-238 for space batteries
facts: Irradiating NpO2 targets with neutrons makes the Pu-238 that powers deep-space probes.
summary: NpO2 is the raw material for spacecraft plutonium-238.

name: Plutonium dioxide

bonding.summary: Pu4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Plutonium gives four electrons to oxygen.

uses: Pu-238 dioxide in radioisotope generators (Voyager, Curiosity)
facts: A pellet of Pu-238 dioxide glows red-hot from its own radioactive decay.
summary: Plutonium dioxide powers spacecraft that travel too far from the Sun for solar panels.

name: Americium dioxide

bonding.summary: Am4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Americium gives four electrons to oxygen.

uses: The radioactive source in ionization smoke detectors
facts: The americium in a smoke detector is AmO2 sealed between gold and silver foils.
summary: AmO2 is the tiny radioactive source inside household smoke detectors.

name: Polonium dioxide

bonding.summary: Po4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Polonium gives four electrons to oxygen.

formation: Po + O2 -> PoO2 (heating polonium in oxygen at 250 °C)
facts: It decomposes back to the elements at about 500 °C.
summary: PoO2 is a rare yellow oxide studied only in milligram amounts.

name: Uranium hexafluoride

bonding.summary: Six U–F bonds pointing to the corners of an octahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Uranium uses all six valence electrons to bond to six fluorines, which pull them strongly. The symmetric molecule is nonpolar and volatile.

facts: UF6 turns straight from solid to gas at 56.5 °C, which lets centrifuges separate U-235 from U-238 as a gas.
hazards: Radioactive; reacts with moisture to form toxic HF.
summary: UF6 is the only uranium compound volatile enough to enrich uranium as a gas.

name: Triuranium octoxide (yellowcake)
aka: yellowcake (when mixed with other uranium oxides)

structure.note: Mixed-valence oxide; real crystal is orthorhombic.

bonding.summary: A mixed-valence oxide with uranium in two oxidation states.
bonding.electronSharing: On average each uranium gives 16/3 electrons to oxygen; formally two are U5+ and one is U6+.

occurrence: The usual product of uranium mills; also in pitchblende.
facts: Despite the name, modern yellowcake is usually dark green to black; the yellow color came from older ammonium diuranate products.
summary: U3O8 is the most stable uranium oxide and the form in which uranium ore concentrate is traded.

name: Titanium dioxide (rutile)

bonding.summary: Each Ti is surrounded by an octahedron of six O; each O by a triangle of three Ti.
bonding.electronSharing: Titanium gives its four valence electrons toward oxygen, with significant covalent sharing.

uses: White pigment in paint, paper, plastics and toothpaste
facts: TiO2 has one of the highest refractive indices of any common material, which is why it is so opaque and white.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine dust is a possible carcinogen when inhaled.
summary: Titanium dioxide is the brightest white pigment, found in most paints.

name: Tin(IV) oxide (cassiterite)

bonding.summary: Rutile structure: tin octahedrally surrounded by oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Tin gives four electrons toward oxygen with partial covalent sharing.

facts: Bronze Age traders shipped tin ore across Europe from Cornwall.
summary: Cassiterite is the ore that made the Bronze Age possible.

name: Calcium titanate (perovskite)

structure.note: Idealized cubic cell; real CaTiO3 is slightly distorted (orthorhombic).

bonding.summary: Ti at the center of an oxygen octahedron, Ca in the spaces between octahedra.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons and titanium four, all ending up on the three oxygens.

occurrence: Found in the Ural Mountains in 1839; rare in crust.
uses: Gives its name to perovskite solar cells
Model for minerals deep in Earth
facts: The most abundant mineral in Earth's lower mantle, bridgmanite, has the perovskite structure.
summary: Perovskite gives its name to one of the most important crystal structures in materials science.

name: Strontium titanate

bonding.summary: The textbook cubic perovskite.
bonding.electronSharing: Strontium gives two electrons and titanium four to the oxygens.

facts: SrTiO3 becomes a superconductor below about 0.3 K.
summary: SrTiO3 is the classic cubic perovskite crystal.

name: Barium titanate

structure.note: Cubic form above 120 °C; slightly tetragonal at room temperature.

bonding.summary: A perovskite in which the Ti ion shifts slightly off-center, creating permanent electric dipoles.
bonding.electronSharing: Barium gives two and titanium four electrons to oxygen; the off-center Ti makes the crystal ferroelectric.

uses: Multilayer ceramic capacitors (billions made each year)
facts: Every smartphone contains hundreds of tiny BaTiO3 capacitors.
summary: Barium titanate's shifting titanium ions make it ferroelectric, perfect for capacitors.

name: Iridium(IV) oxide

bonding.summary: Rutile structure, but metallic: its partly filled 5d band conducts electricity.
bonding.electronSharing: Iridium gives four electrons toward oxygen; its remaining 5d electrons are shared through the crystal like a metal.

formation: Ir + O2 -> IrO2 (heating iridium in air)
uses: Anode catalyst for splitting water in PEM electrolyzers
facts: IrO2 is one of the few catalysts that survive the harsh acid of green-hydrogen electrolyzers; it decomposes near 1,100 °C.
summary: IrO2 is a conductive oxide that catalyzes oxygen release in green-hydrogen production.
